<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 9203, the Student Protection and University Accountability Act, amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA), adding requirements related to compliance with title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VI) to the Provisional Participation Agreement (PPA) institutions of higher education (IHEs) enter into in order to receive access to Federal Student Aid. The bill also makes changes to the process by which the U.S. Department of Education (Department or ED) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) handles Title VI claims. While we appreciate the spirit in which the bill is offered, we have concerns about specific provisions in the bill that may increase the backlog of cases at OCR and could result in inequitable outcomes between complaints based in Title VI and other education civil rights cases.
In evaluating a substantially similar bill last Congress, the Civil Rights Protection Act,\1\ our Minority Views focused on the actions of the Committee in relation to Title VI in the 118th Congress.\2\ Committee Democrats remain concerned the Majority has taken a narrow view of the scope of Title VI in its choice of hearings and oversight activity this Congress.\3\ However, the Committee's actions have been greatly overshadowed by the Administration's actions in education civil rights generally, Title VI specifically. Taken in total, these actions suggest that this administration cannot be given any additional authority over Title VI from Congress until substantial oversight has been conducted on how it has wielded, and surpassed its authority so far.
\1\H.R. 8648, 118th Cong., (2024).
\2\H.R. Rep. No. 118-593 at 38-43 (``We fervently hope that the Committee is able to get answers from schools to the allegations of antisemitism on their campuses that it has requested. There is no justification for threats, violence, harassment, or intimidation against any student on campus, especially if such threats are the result of their shared ancestry, national origin, or ethnic characteristics. The Committee's failure to address any such accusation of threats, violence, harassment, or intimidation against any Muslim student on any campus in America in the wake of October 7th does not change this hope, but it does raise significant concern. We fear this oversight failure on the Committee's part will solidify the impression that this Committee is not interested in ensuring that all students have safe, nurturing learning environments.'').
\3\E.g. From Playground to Classroom: The Spread of Antisemitism in K-12 Schools Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Early Childhood, Elementary & Secondary Educ. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong.
(2025) (statement of Ranking Member Rep. Suzanne Bonamici) (``Instead of offering any real solutions, Republicans use antisemitism as an excuse to turn our nation's civil rights laws upside down and undermine public education. We have seen this most prominently with higher education, and it is clear the committee is now seeking to do the same thing to our local public elementary, middle, and high schools. The reality is that the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans are using the real plight of Jewish students experiencing antisemitism to destabilize institutions they don't approve of, whether institutions of higher education or teachers' unions.'').
H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE DISMANTLING OF ED OCR AND CIVIL RIGHTS
ENFORCEMENT
President Trump ran for re-election in part on a promise to shut down the U.S. Department of Education.\4\ A bi-partisan consensus of legal scholars agrees this is an act the President does not have the power to do.\5\ Nevertheless, his Administration is attempting to abolish the Department, with little apparent regard for the statutory duties Congress has placed on the Department and its offices. This is nowhere more obvious or impactful than in the Department's Office for Civil Rights.
\4\E.g., Graham Kates, Can Trump Dismantle the Department of Education? It Won't be Easy, Experts Say, CBS News (Feb. 4, 2025), https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-dismantle-education-department/; Time Staff, Read the Full Transcript of Donald Trump's 2024 Person of the Year Interview with TIME, TIME (Dec. 12, 2024), https://time.com/6972022/donald-trump-transcript-2024-election/.
\5\E.g., Laura Mannweiler, Can Trump Really Dissolve A Government Agency?, USNews, Feb. 11, 2025, https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/ articles/2025-02-11/can-trump-really-dissolve-a-government-agency-like-usaid-or-the-department-of-education.
OCR is the specific office charged in statute with enforcing Title VI education cases.\6\ OCR was one of the offices that lost the most employees (in both number and percentage) as a result of the Department's reduction-in-force in 2025.\7\ The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) documented how the Department paid OCR employees as much as $38 million to not work last year.\8\ The Senate HELP Committee Minority Staff recently reported that in 2025, OCR had lowest rate of resolved cases in over a decade, including zero resolution agreements in cases of racial harassment and discriminatory school discipline.\9\ The same Chairman that called up H.R. 9203 for consideration recently championed the interagency agreement (IAA) that sent the majority of OCR's investigatory work to the Department of Justice.\10\ It remains puzzling that this majority purports to champion civil rights enforcement while simultaneously supporting the destruction of the office charged with enforcing educational civil rights.
\6\Department of Education Organization Act, Pub. L. No. 96-88
Sec.  203, 93 Stat. 669 (1979).
\7\See U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of the Inspector Gen., FLASH REPORT Review of U.S. Department of Education Changes in Staffing and Operations 5, June 2026, https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/ documents/reports/2026-06/FY26%20F25DC0245%20%286.22.26%29v100_508_ SECURED.pdf (showing OCR lost a total number of employees second only to the Office of Federal Student Aid, and ranked 6th out of the 16 ED offices affected by the reduction in force by percentage of employees lost).
\8\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-26-108320, Department of Education: Full Costs and Savings Estimate Needed for Reduction-in- Force and Restructuring of the Office for Civil Rights 2 (2026), https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-108320.pdf.
\9\S. Comm. on Health, Educ., Lab., & Pensions, Minority Staff, Justice Denied: How Trump's Office for Civil Rights Reached a 12-Year Low in Protecting Students from Discrimination, (Apr. 28, 2026), https://www.sanders.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/ 04.24.26-Justice-Denied-How-Trumps-Office-for-Civil-Rights-Reached-a- 12-Year-Low-in-Protecting-Students-from- Discrimination_FINAL.pdf.
\10\Press Release, H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, Chairman Walberg Praises Trump for Putting Students First, Cutting Bureaucracy (June 16, 2026), https://edworkforce.house.gov/news/ documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=413416.
Concurrent with this slowdown in complaint and case management, OCR has refocused its reduced capacity on a few key, politicized areas: Title IX cases where schools and colleges allow transgender students access to facilities or sports teams consistent with their gender identity; Title VI cases involving programming related to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI); and Title VI cases involving allegations of antisemitism.\11\ This is consistent with the warped approach to Title VI that has been embraced across Departments by this Administration.
\11\Rachel M. Perera, How the US Department of Education Has Turned Civil Rights Enforcement into a Discriminatory Tool, BROOKINGS, Feb. 20, 2026, https://www.brookings.edu/ articles/how-the-us-department-of-education-has-turned-civil-rights-enforcement-into-a-discriminatory-tool/.
H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE WARPING OF TITLE VI FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES
The administration hit the ground running on February 14, 2025, when the Department promulgated guidance in the form of a Dear Colleague Letter (DCL) that threatened to take away funding from any school that went beyond what they believed were the bounds of the Supreme Court's decision in Students for Fair Admissions (SFFA).\12\ In that case,the Court ruled against Harvard University's and the University of North Carolina's admissions processes that used race as one of many factors in college admissions decisions, saying they violated Title VI.\13\ The Court noted the decision was narrowly tailored to the controversy before it.\14\ However, in its guidance to schools, ED claimed that the SFFA decision went beyond admissions touching any consideration of race, including DEI, in education generally.\15\ Further, ED would have required schools to certify that they were complying with the viewpoints expressed in the guidance, leaving them liable to litigation if they were found to have certified falsely.\16\
\12\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Dear Colleague Letter: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act in Light of Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (Feb. 14, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/ document/dear-colleague-letter-sffa-v-harvard-109506.pdf; Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023).
\13\Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181, 230
(2023).
\14\600 U.S. at 208 (``These cases involve whether a university may make admissions decisions that turn on an applicant's race.''); 600 U.S. at 343 (``Answering the question whether Harvard's and UNC's policies survive strict scrutiny under settled law is straightforward, both because of the procedural posture of these cases and because of the narrow scope of the issues presented by petitioner Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.'') (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
\15\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Dear Colleague Letter: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act in Light of Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (Feb. 14, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/ document/dear-colleague-letter-sffa-v-harvard-109506.pdf (``Although SFFA addressed admissions decisions, the Supreme Court's holding applies more broadly. At its core, the test is simple: If an educational institution treats a person of one race differently than it treats another person because of that person's race, the educational institution violates the law.'').
\16\Id.; U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Reminder of Legal Obligations Undertaken in Exchange for Receiving Federal Financial Assistance and Request for Certification Under Title VI and SFFA v. Harvard (April 3, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/document/reminder-of-legal-obligations-undertaken-exchange-receiving-federal-financial-assistance-and-request-certification-under-title-vi-and-sffa-v-harvard-april- 3.pdf.
The National Education Association (NEA), American Federation of Teachers (AFT), and NAACP all brought suits challenging the guidance and the certification requirement in different federal courts as violations of both federal law and the Constitution.\17\ After the AFT succeeded in having the DCL and its certification requirement vacated, the declined to appeal that case, and filed joint motions to dismiss the NEA and NAACP cases.\18\ This did not stop the Administration from trying to further their goals on Title VI by other means. Regulatory actions at the General Services Administration and the Office of Management and Budget have both attempted to force recipients of federal assistance to certify their adherence to the Administrations' interpretations of Title VI and civil rights more broadly.\19\
\17\Nat'l Educ. Ass'n v. Dep't of Educ., 1:25-cv-0091 (D. N.H., Mar. 5, 2005); Am. Fed'n of Teachers v. Dep't of Educ., 1:25-cv-00628 (D. Md., Feb. 25, 2025); NAACP v. Dep't of Educ., 1:25-cv-01120 (D. D.C., Apr. 15, 2025).
